name: Chapter 6: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion
description: Centre of mass, cross product, torque, angular momentum, equilibrium, moment of inertia, rotational kinematics and dynamics, rolling

cards.term: What is a rigid body?
cards.definition: A body whose shape never changes: the distance between every pair of particles stays fixed. No real body is perfectly rigid

cards.term: What is pure translation?
cards.definition: Every particle of the body has the same velocity at any instant

cards.term: Why is a rolling cylinder not in pure translation?
cards.definition: Its points have different velocities; the contact point is momentarily at rest

cards.term: In rotation about a fixed axis, how does each particle move?
cards.definition: In a circle in a plane ⟂ to the axis, centred on the axis. Points on the axis stay at rest

cards.term: What is precession? Example?
cards.definition: The axis of a spinning body sweeps out a cone about the vertical; a spinning top (only its tip is fixed)

cards.term: Motion of a rigid body that is pivoted vs not pivoted?
cards.definition: Pivoted/fixed: rotation only. Free: pure translation, or translation + rotation

cards.term: Centre of mass of two particles on the x-axis?
cards.definition: \[X = \dfrac{m_1x_1 + m_2x_2}{m_1 + m_2}\]a mass-weighted mean; midway if masses are equal

cards.term: Centre of mass of n particles (vector form)?
cards.definition: \[\vec R = \dfrac{\sum m_i \vec r_i}{M}\]M = total mass

cards.term: CM of a continuous body?
cards.definition: \[\vec R = \dfrac{1}{M}\int \vec r\,dm\]if the origin is at the CM, ∫r dm = 0

cards.term: CM of three equal masses at the corners of a triangle?
cards.definition: At the centroid of the triangle

cards.term: Where is the CM of a uniform rod, ring, disc, sphere, cube?
cards.definition: At the geometric centre, by reflection symmetry

cards.term: Must the CM lie inside the body? (Exercise 6.1)
cards.definition: No: e.g. a ring, hollow sphere, hollow cylinder have their CM in empty space

cards.term: Example 6.1: 100 g, 150 g, 200 g at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side 0.5 m (100 g at origin, 150 g at (0.5, 0)). CM?
cards.definition: X = 5/18 m, Y = 1/(3√3) m — not the geometric centre, as the masses differ

cards.term: Example 6.2: CM of a triangular lamina?
cards.definition: At the centroid: each strip parallel to a side has its CM on the median, so the CM lies on all three medians

cards.term: Example 6.3: uniform L-shaped lamina of three 1 m squares (3 kg). CM?
cards.definition: (5/6 m, 5/6 m): on the line of symmetry OD

cards.term: Exercise 6.2: HCl, bond 1.27 Å, Cl is 35.5 × H. Location of the CM?
cards.definition: 1.24 Å from the H nucleus (very close to Cl)

cards.term: Teacher addition: CM of a uniform semicircular ring and disc (radius R) from the centre?
cards.definition: Ring: \( \dfrac{2R}{\pi} \); disc: \( \dfrac{4R}{3\pi} \)

cards.term: Exercise 6.15: a hole of radius R/2 is cut from a disc of radius R, centred R/2 from the centre. CM of the rest?
cards.definition: R/6 from the centre, on the side opposite the hole (treat the hole as negative mass)

cards.term: Equation of motion of the centre of mass?
cards.definition: \[M\vec A = \vec F_{ext}\]the CM moves as if all mass were there and all external forces acted there

cards.term: Why do internal forces not affect the CM?
cards.definition: By the third law they come in equal and opposite pairs and cancel in the sum

cards.term: Exploding projectile: path of the centre of mass
cards.definition: Internal explosion forces do not affect the CM; with gravity alone acting, the CM continues on the original parabola

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Centre of mass · explosion

A shell explodes into two equal pieces at the top of its path. What path does the centre of mass follow?

Which forces are external?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Centre of mass · explosion

A shell explodes into two equal pieces at the top of its path. What path does the centre of mass follow?

The explosion forces are internal; the only external force is still gravity (Mg).

So Macm = Mg: the CM continues on the same parabola as if nothing happened.

cards.term: Total momentum of a system and the CM velocity?
cards.definition: \( \vec P = M\vec V \) ; \( \dfrac{d\vec P}{dt} = \vec F_{ext} \) (second law for a system)

cards.term: If the net external force is zero?
cards.definition: Total momentum is conserved and the CM moves with constant velocity

cards.term: Radium nucleus decays into radon + α. Seen from the CM frame?
cards.definition: The two products fly apart back to back; the CM stays at rest (or keeps moving uniformly in the lab)

cards.term: Binary stars: what do their paths look like in the CM frame?
cards.definition: Circles about the CM, diametrically opposite; in the lab, circles + uniform drift of the CM

cards.term: Exercise 6.3: a child runs about on a trolley moving at V on a smooth floor. Speed of the CM of (trolley + child)?
cards.definition: Still V: the running forces are internal

cards.term: Useful split of kinetic energy of a system (Points to ponder)?
cards.definition: \[K = K' + \tfrac12 MV^2\]KE about the CM + KE of the CM

cards.term: Define the vector (cross) product a × b.
cards.definition: Magnitude \( ab\sin\theta \), direction ⟂ to both a and b by the right-hand rule (curl fingers from a to b; thumb gives c)

cards.term: Is the cross product commutative?
cards.definition: No:\[\vec b \times \vec a = -\vec a \times \vec b\]

cards.term: a × a = ?
cards.definition: The null vector (sin 0 = 0)

cards.text: î × ĵ = {{c1::k̂}}, ĵ × k̂ = {{c2::î}}, k̂ × î = {{c3::ĵ}}; in reverse order the sign is negative.

cards.term: Mnemonic for unit-vector cross products?
cards.definition: Write i → j → k → i in a circle: going clockwise gives +, anticlockwise gives −

cards.term: a × b in components?
cards.definition: Determinant with rows (î ĵ k̂), (aₓ aᵧ a𝓏), (bₓ bᵧ b𝓏)

cards.term: Example 6.4: a = 3î − 4ĵ + 5k̂, b = −2î + ĵ − 3k̂. a·b and a × b?
cards.definition: a·b = −25; a × b = 7î − ĵ − 5k̂

cards.term: Does a × b change sign under reflection?
cards.definition: No: both a and b flip sign, so a × b does not (it is an axial vector)

cards.term: Exercise 6.4: area of the triangle formed by a and b?
cards.definition: \[\tfrac12 |\vec a \times \vec b|\]

cards.term: Exercise 6.5: what does a·(b × c) represent?
cards.definition: The volume of the parallelepiped on a, b, c

cards.term: Relation between linear and angular velocity (vector form)?
cards.definition: \( \vec v = \vec\omega \times \vec r \) ; magnitude \( v = \omega r_\perp \)

cards.term: Direction of the angular velocity vector?
cards.definition: Along the axis, the way a right-handed screw turning with the body would advance

cards.term: What characterises pure rotation about a fixed axis?
cards.definition: Every particle has the same angular velocity (but different linear speeds, ∝ distance from the axis)

cards.term: Define angular acceleration.
cards.definition: \[\vec\alpha = \dfrac{d\vec\omega}{dt}\]for a fixed axis, α = dω/dt (scalar)

cards.term: Why does pushing a door at the hinge not open it?
cards.definition: Rotation depends on where and how the force acts, not the force alone: at the hinge the lever arm is zero

cards.term: Define torque (moment of force).
cards.definition: \( \vec\tau = \vec r \times \vec F \); \( \tau = rF\sin\theta = r_\perp F \)

cards.term: Unit and dimensions of torque; is it the same as work?
cards.definition: N m, [M L² T⁻²] like work, but torque is a vector and is never called joule

cards.term: When is the torque of a force zero?
cards.definition: F = 0, r = 0, or the line of action passes through the origin (θ = 0° or 180°)

cards.term: Example 6.5: τ of F = 7î + 3ĵ − 5k̂ acting at r = î − ĵ + k̂?
cards.definition: 2î + 12ĵ + 10k̂

cards.term: Define the angular momentum of a particle.
cards.definition: \( \vec l = \vec r \times \vec p \) ; \( l = rp\sin\theta = r_\perp p \)

cards.term: Relation between torque and angular momentum?
cards.definition: \[\dfrac{d\vec l}{dt} = \vec\tau\]the rotational analogue of F = dp/dt

cards.term: For a system, which torques change L?
cards.definition: Only external torques: \( \dfrac{d\vec L}{dt} = \vec\tau_{ext} \) (internal forces along the joining lines cancel)

cards.term: State conservation of angular momentum.
cards.definition: If \( \vec\tau_{ext} = 0 \), L is constant (each component separately)

cards.term: Example 6.6: angular momentum of a particle moving with constant velocity, about any point?
cards.definition: Constant: r sin θ (perpendicular distance of the line of motion) and p stay fixed; no torque acts

cards.term: Exercise 6.6: components of l = r × p?
cards.definition: \[l_x = yp_z - zp_y,\ l_y = zp_x - xp_z,\ l_z = xp_y - yp_x\]motion in the x-y plane gives only l𝓏

cards.term: Bicycle-rim experiment: spinning rim held by one string. What happens?
cards.definition: Instead of falling, its axis (angular momentum) precesses about the string

cards.term: Conditions for mechanical equilibrium of a rigid body?
cards.definition: Translational: ΣF = 0. Rotational: Στ = 0

cards.term: How many conditions for coplanar forces?
cards.definition: Three: two force components and one torque component (⟂ to the plane)

cards.term: Equal parallel forces, same direction, at the ends of a light rod?
cards.definition: Rotational equilibrium but not translational

cards.term: What is a couple? Effect?
cards.definition: Two equal and opposite forces with different lines of action: rotation without translation

cards.term: Two examples of a couple?
cards.definition: Fingers turning a bottle lid; Earth’s field on a compass needle

cards.term: Example 6.7: does the moment of a couple depend on the reference point?
cards.definition: No: moment = AB × F for any origin

cards.term: When is total torque independent of the origin?
cards.definition: When the total external force is zero

cards.term: Principle of moments for a lever?
cards.definition: \[d_1F_1 = d_2F_2\]load arm × load = effort arm × effort

cards.term: Mechanical advantage of a lever?
cards.definition: \[MA = \dfrac{F_1}{F_2} = \dfrac{d_2}{d_1}\]> 1 when the effort arm is longer than the load arm

cards.term: Define the centre of gravity.
cards.definition: The point about which the total gravitational torque on the body is zero

cards.term: When do the centre of gravity and centre of mass coincide?
cards.definition: When g is uniform over the body. For a very tall body (g varies) they differ

cards.term: How to find the CG of an irregular lamina by suspension?
cards.definition: Hang it from two or three points; the verticals through the suspension points meet at the CG

cards.term: Bar on two knife edges: reactions
cards.definition: R₁ + R₂ = 98 N and R₁ − R₂ = 11.76 N give R₁ ≈ 55 N, R₂ ≈ 43 N

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 6.8 · knife edges

Find the missing step.

70 cm, 4.00 kg bar on knife edges 10 cm from each end; 6.00 kg hung 30 cm from end A. Reactions?
  1. R₁ + R₂ = 10.00g = 98.0 N
  2. ?
  3. R₁ − R₂ = 1.2g = 11.76 N
  4. R₁ ≈ 55 N, R₂ ≈ 43 N
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 6.8 · knife edges

Find the missing step.

70 cm, 4.00 kg bar on knife edges 10 cm from each end; 6.00 kg hung 30 cm from end A. Reactions?
  1. R₁ + R₂ = 10.00g = 98.0 N
  2. Moments about G: −0.25R₁ + 0.05 × 6g + 0.25R₂ = 0
  3. R₁ − R₂ = 1.2g = 11.76 N
  4. R₁ ≈ 55 N, R₂ ≈ 43 N

cards.term: Example 6.8: why take moments about G?
cards.definition: The rod’s own weight then has zero moment, removing one unknown term

cards.term: Example 6.9: 3 m, 20 kg ladder on a frictionless wall, foot 1 m out. Reactions?
cards.definition: Wall F₁ = 34.6 N; floor: N = 196 N, friction 34.6 N, total ≈ 199 N at ≈ 80° to the horizontal

cards.term: Exercise 6.9: 1800 kg car, axles 1.8 m apart, CG 1.05 m behind the front axle. Force on each front and back wheel?
cards.definition: Front 3675 N each; back 5145 N each

cards.term: Exercise 6.16: two 5 g coins at the 12.0 cm mark shift the balance point of a metre stick to 45.0 cm. Mass of the stick?
cards.definition: 66.0 g (10 g × 33 cm = m × 5 cm)

cards.term: Exercise 6.8: bar hung by strings at 36.9° and 53.1° to the vertical, length 2 m. CG from the left end?
cards.definition: 72 cm

cards.term: Define moment of inertia.
cards.definition: \[I = \sum m_i r_i^2\](rᵢ = perpendicular distance from the axis); unit kg m²

cards.term: Rotational kinetic energy?
cards.definition: \[K = \tfrac12 I\omega^2\]

cards.term: Why is I the rotational analogue of mass?
cards.definition: It measures resistance to change in rotational motion, just as mass does for translation (compare ½Iω² with ½mv²)

cards.term: Does a body have a fixed moment of inertia like its mass?
cards.definition: No: I depends on the axis and on how mass is distributed about it

cards.term: I of a pair of masses M/2 on a light rod of length l, about the perpendicular axis through the centre?
Moments of inertia (Table 6.1, part 1)
cards.definition: Ring, ⟂ axis through centre: MR²; Ring, about a diameter: MR²/2; Thin rod, ⟂ axis at midpoint: ML²/12; Disc, ⟂ axis through centre: MR²/2; Disc, about a diameter: MR²/4

cards.definition: Hollow cylinder, own axis: MR²; Solid cylinder, own axis: MR²/2; Solid sphere, diameter: 2MR²/5; Teacher addition: hollow sphere, diameter: 2MR²/3; Teacher addition: rod about one end: ML²/3

advancedHtml.frontHtml:

Hollow cylinder, own axis?
Solid cylinder, own axis?
Solid sphere, diameter?
Teacher addition: hollow sphere, diameter?
Teacher addition: rod about one end?

Teacher addition: hollow sphere, diameter2MR²/3
Teacher addition: rod about one endML²/3

cards.term: Identify: which shapes in Table 6.1 have the largest and smallest I for the same M and R?
cards.definition: Largest: ring / hollow cylinder (MR²); smallest: disc about a diameter (MR²/4)

cards.term: Mnemonic: why does a ring have more I than a disc of the same mass and radius?
cards.definition: All the ring’s mass sits at the rim (distance R); the disc’s mass is spread inwards: "mass far out, spin hard to start"

cards.term: Define radius of gyration.
cards.definition: \( I = Mk^2 \): k is the distance at which the whole mass, as a point, would give the same I

cards.term: Radius of gyration of a rod (⟂ axis at centre) and a disc (about a diameter)?
cards.definition: \( k = \dfrac{L}{\sqrt{12}} \) and \( k = \dfrac{R}{2} \)

cards.term: What is a flywheel and why is it used?
cards.definition: A disc with large I in engines; it resists sudden changes of speed, giving smooth motion

cards.term: Teacher addition (not in rationalised NCERT, needed for JEE): parallel axis theorem?
cards.definition: \[I = I_{cm} + Md^2\]for a parallel axis at distance d from the axis through the CM

cards.term: Teacher addition: perpendicular axis theorem?
cards.definition: \[I_z = I_x + I_y\]for a plane lamina (x, y in its plane, z ⟂ through the same point)

cards.term: Teacher addition: I of a disc about a tangent in its plane?
cards.definition: \[\tfrac14 MR^2 + MR^2 = \tfrac54 MR^2\](perpendicular then parallel axis theorem)

cards.text: Equations of rotational motion with constant α: {{c1::ω = ω₀ + αt}}, {{c2::θ = θ₀ + ω₀t + ½αt²}}, {{c3::ω² = ω₀² + 2α(θ − θ₀)}}.

cards.term: How many degrees of freedom does rotation about a fixed axis have?
cards.definition: One (the angle θ), like motion along a line

cards.term: Motor wheel: angular acceleration and revolutions
cards.definition: α = 4π rad/s²; θ = 1152π rad = 576 revolutions

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 6.11 · motor wheel

Find the missing step.

A motor goes from 1200 rpm to 3120 rpm in 16 s (uniform). α and revolutions?
  1. ω₀ = 2π × 1200/60 = 40π rad/s; ω = 104π rad/s
  2. α = (104π − 40π)/16 = 4π rad/s²
  3. ?
  4. 576 revolutions
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 6.11 · motor wheel

Find the missing step.

A motor goes from 1200 rpm to 3120 rpm in 16 s (uniform). α and revolutions?
  1. ω₀ = 2π × 1200/60 = 40π rad/s; ω = 104π rad/s
  2. α = (104π − 40π)/16 = 4π rad/s²
  3. θ = 40π × 16 + ½ × 4π × 16² = 1152π rad
  4. 576 revolutions

cards.term: Trap: converting rpm to rad/s?
cards.definition: Multiply by 2π/60: 1200 rpm = 20 rev/s = 40π rad/s

cards.term: Which forces matter for rotation about a fixed axis?
cards.definition: Only components in planes ⟂ to the axis, with position vectors ⟂ to the axis; the rest are cancelled by the constraint forces of the bearings

cards.term: Work and power of a torque?
cards.definition: \[dW = \tau\,d\theta,\quad P = \tau\omega\]

cards.term: Newton’s second law for rotation about a fixed axis?
cards.definition: \[\tau = I\alpha\]

cards.term: Translational and rotational analogues (Table 6.2)
cards.definition: Mass M: moment of inertia I; Force F = Ma: torque τ = Iα; Work F ds: τ dθ; KE ½Mv²: ½Iω²; Power Fv: τω; Momentum Mv: L = Iω

cards.term: Flywheel pulled by a cord
cards.definition: α = 5/0.4 = 12.5 rad/s²; work 50 J = rotational KE gained (no friction)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 6.12 · flywheel

Find the missing step.

25 N pull on a cord round a 20 kg, 20 cm radius flywheel (disc) from rest. α, work and KE after 2 m of cord?
  1. τ = FR = 25 × 0.2 = 5 N m; I = ½MR² = 0.4 kg m²
  2. ?
  3. W = F × 2 m = 50 J; θ = 2/0.2 = 10 rad
  4. ω² = 2αθ = 250 → KE = ½Iω² = 50 J = W
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 6.12 · flywheel

Find the missing step.

25 N pull on a cord round a 20 kg, 20 cm radius flywheel (disc) from rest. α, work and KE after 2 m of cord?
  1. τ = FR = 25 × 0.2 = 5 N m; I = ½MR² = 0.4 kg m²
  2. α = τ/I = 12.5 rad/s²
  3. W = F × 2 m = 50 J; θ = 2/0.2 = 10 rad
  4. ω² = 2αθ = 250 → KE = ½Iω² = 50 J = W

cards.term: Exercise 6.10: equal torques on a hollow cylinder and a solid sphere (same M, R). Which spins faster after a time?
cards.definition: The sphere: smaller I (2MR²/5 < MR²), so larger α

cards.term: Exercise 6.13: 30 N pulls a rope on a 3 kg hollow cylinder of radius 40 cm. α and linear acceleration of the rope?
cards.definition: α = 30 × 0.4 / (3 × 0.16) = 25 rad/s²; a = αR = 10 m/s²

cards.term: Exercise 6.14: torque 180 N m at 200 rad/s. Power?
cards.definition: P = τω = 36 kW

cards.term: Exercise 6.11: solid cylinder 20 kg, R = 0.25 m, ω = 100 rad/s. KE and L?
cards.definition: I = 0.625 kg m²; KE = 3125 J, L = 62.5 J s

cards.term: Angular momentum about a fixed axis?
cards.definition: \( L_z = I\omega \); for bodies symmetric about the axis, L = Iω along the axis

cards.term: Are l and ω always parallel?
cards.definition: No: for a single particle or an unsymmetric body, L is not along the axis; only for a symmetric body is L = Iω

cards.term: Law for fixed-axis rotation with changing I?
cards.definition: \[\dfrac{d(I\omega)}{dt} = \tau\]with τ = 0: Iω = constant

cards.term: Arms in, spin faster: Iω = constant
cards.definition: No external torque so Iω is constant; pulling arms in reduces I and increases ω (KE rises by the work of the muscles)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Conservation of angular momentum

A person spins on a frictionless swivel chair holding two weights. What happens when the arms are pulled in?

What stays constant?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Conservation of angular momentum

A person spins on a frictionless swivel chair holding two weights. What happens when the arms are pulled in?

No external torque → L = Iω = constant. Pulling the mass inward cuts I, so ω rises.

Skaters, divers and dancers doing a pirouette use this. Rotational KE = L²/2I increases: the muscles do work pulling the arms in.

cards.term: Why do divers and acrobats curl up in mid-air?
cards.definition: Curling up reduces I, so ω rises (L conserved) and they complete more somersaults

cards.term: Swivel-chair demonstration?
cards.definition: Stretching the arms slows the spin, pulling them in speeds it up (Iω constant)

cards.term: Exercise 6.12: a child on a turntable at 40 rpm reduces I to 2/5. New speed and KE?
cards.definition: 100 rpm; KE becomes 2.5×: the child’s internal energy does the work

cards.term: Exercise 6.17: O₂ molecule, I = 1.94 × 10⁻⁴⁶ kg m², m = 5.30 × 10⁻²⁶ kg, v = 500 m/s, rotational KE = ⅔ translational KE. ω?
cards.definition: 6.75 × 10¹² rad/s

cards.term: Teacher addition (dropped from rationalised NCERT, still in JEE): condition for rolling without slipping?
cards.definition: \[v_{cm} = R\omega\]the contact point is instantaneously at rest

cards.term: Rolling without slipping: speeds of top, centre and contact point
cards.definition: Top moves at 2v, centre at v, contact point at 0 (v = Rω); a rim point traces a cycloid

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Rolling motion · intuition

A wheel rolls without slipping at speed v. How fast do its top, centre and contact point move? What path does a rim point trace?

Rolling = sliding + spinning.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Rolling motion · intuition

A wheel rolls without slipping at speed v. How fast do its top, centre and contact point move? What path does a rim point trace?

Rolling = translation (v) + rotation (Rω = v). Top: v + v = 2v; centre: v; contact: v − v = 0.

A rim point traces a cycloid (dashed) and touches the ground at rest each turn.

cards.term: Speeds of the top point, centre and contact point of a rolling wheel?
cards.definition: 2v, v, 0

cards.term: Kinetic energy of a rolling body?
cards.definition: \[K = \tfrac12 mv^2 + \tfrac12 I\omega^2 = \tfrac12 mv^2\left(1 + \dfrac{k^2}{R^2}\right)\]

cards.term: Acceleration of a body rolling down an incline of angle θ?
cards.definition: \[a = \dfrac{g\sin\theta}{1 + k^2/R^2}\]

cards.term: Which rolls down an incline first?
cards.definition: Solid sphere: 2/5 — fastest; Solid cylinder / disc: 1/2 — second; Hollow sphere: 2/3 — third; Ring / hollow cylinder: 1 — slowest

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Teacher addition · rolling race

k²/R² and order down an incline?

Solid sphere?
Solid cylinder / disc?
Hollow sphere?
Ring / hollow cylinder?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Teacher addition · rolling race

k²/R² and order down an incline?

Solid sphere2/5 — fastest
Solid cylinder / disc1/2 — second
Hollow sphere2/3 — third
Ring / hollow cylinder1 — slowest

Smaller k²/R² → less energy locked in rotation → faster. Mass and radius do not matter.

cards.term: Chapter 6 concept checks
cards.definition: Internal forces can change the CM motion: False; Zero net force ⇒ zero net torque: False (couple); CG = CM always: False (only in uniform g); To prove dL/dt = τext you need the third law with central forces: True; Torque about any origin is the same if net force is zero: True

Zero net force ⇒ zero net torque?
CG = CM always?
